items.title: Evaluating Social Reasoning in Embodied Vision-Language Models
items.abstract: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.

items.title: Evolution of University Students’ AI Dependency and Creativity in the Technology Diffusion Process: A Four-Wave Repeated Cross-Sectional Study in China
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping higher education, yet potential risks accompany over-reliance on these tools. Grounded in Rogers’ diffusion-of-innovations theory, the present study employed a mixed-methods design. Four waves of independent cross-sectional quantitative data (T1–T4, N = 788) were complemented by semi-structured interviews with 20 undergraduate students. Key patterns emerged as follows: (i) Across later waves, the direct association between external regulation and intrinsic motivation attenuated, while the indirect association operating via identified regulation strengthened. The path from identified regulation to intrinsic motivation was the only relationship that demonstrated significant cross-pair differences while satisfying invariance requirements for all three wave-pair comparisons. Because scalar invariance could not be established, this pattern is interpreted solely as a descriptive group-level temporal trend and should not be read as evidence of intra-individual change. (ii) AI-assisted creativity showed the largest and most consistent downward shift: estimates in later waves were significantly lower relative to the T1 baseline, with effect sizes increasing progressively (Δ = −0.391 to −0.549; d = −0.61 to −0.95; all p < 0.001 following Holm correction). This pattern remained largely unchanged after adjusting for gender, year of study, and academic major, and held up in four predefined subsamples as well as under propensity-score weighting. (iii) The linkage between AI dependency and creativity was significantly positive only at T3 and became negative but non-significant at T4, pointing to a conditional, wave-specific association rather than a stable linear relationship. (iv) Observed wave-level differences for AI dependency and intrinsic motivation did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons. Sensitivity tests yielded only two significant coefficients for AI dependency and none for intrinsic motivation; accordingly, these fluctuations are not given substantive theoretical interpretation. Retrospective qualitative accounts provided supplementary process-oriented context: participants reported initial exposure to AI driven by prevailing social trends, sustained use based on perceived utility, subsequent disappointment in unreliable or misleading outputs, and eventual shifts toward more strategic, self-regulated engagement. Given their retrospective nature, interview narratives were not used to triangulate or validate the quantitative findings. Collectively, this work suggests that as AI-supported learning becomes normalized within a diffusion-driven context, group-level indicators of students’ subjective creative experiences tend to decline. Higher-education institutions may therefore prioritize protecting learners’ creative agency as an explicit educational goal.

items.title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
items.abstract: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s.

items.title: Expertise modulates automation bias and sentinel behavior in human–AI collaborative diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum
items.abstract: Medical AI is often validated under an additive assumption that algorithmic sensitivity and clinician oversight will combine to improve care. We tested this assumption in the high-stakes diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum, a time-critical surgical emergency. In a multi-reader crossover study analyzing 1750 interpretation events, clinicians reviewed radiographs aided by either a high-reliability model or a systematically error-injected model. We found that high AI reliability paradoxically induces automation bias in trainees, who accepted 52.0% of incorrect suggestions, while offering limited gains to experts. Conversely, when challenged by flawed AI, the three participating neonatologists exhibited a “sentinel behavior” phenotype, correctly overriding 91.7% of errors (Wilson 95% CI: 83.0–96.0%) consistent with increased deliberation; given the small specialist cohort, this finding is hypothesis-generating and warrants prospective replication. We operationalize systemic resilience as the capacity to maintain diagnostic integrity under algorithmic failure and demonstrate that clinical validity depends on the human–AI team’s adversarial resilience rather than standalone accuracy. To mitigate the risk of deskilling and never-skilling, we release an open-source educational sandbox designed to inoculate clinicians against automated errors.

items.title: Explainable AI for Detecting Safety Barrier Degradation from Near Miss Reports
items.abstract: Industrial maintenance generates near miss narratives that may reveal weaknesses in energy isolation, equipment integrity, permit coordination and other safety barriers. However, interpreting these reports requires contextual judgement, and an automated summary can conceal missing evidence or produce unjustified conclusions. This conceptual paper proposes an evidence-linked artificial intelligence framework for identifying reported barrier degradation and supporting accountable human review. The framework combines a controlled barrier taxonomy, source-linked extraction, retrieval from approved site documents, uncertainty handling and verification of corrective actions. Its central research proposition is that the value of AI should be evaluated through the quality of barrier decisions and the completeness of supporting evidence, rather than classification accuracy alone. A staged mixed methods protocol is specified, including expert annotation, temporal and site-separated testing, comparison with simpler methods, a randomised reviewer study and a prospective shadow deployment. Primary outcomes concern detection of expert-adjudicated barrier concerns, unsupported assertions and reviewer decision quality. Incident reduction is reserved for later investigation and is not inferred from report processing performance. No field dataset, implemented prototype or empirical results are presented. The contribution is a testable research design that connects explainable AI with practical safety assurance while retaining operational authority with competent personnel

items.title: Explainable Decision Graphs for Trustworthy Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are in-creasingly being considered for critical applications such as healthcare, finance, cybersecurity, and autonomous transporta-tion. These systems consist of multiple intelligent agents that can independently perceive information, reason about their environment, communicate with other agents, and execute deci-sions. Although multi-agent architectures provide flexibility and scalability, their distributed decision-making process can make the overall system difficult to understand, audit, and verify. Existing Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques such as Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) primarily fo-cus on explaining individual machine-learning predictions. They provide limited support for representing collaborative reasoning, inter-agent communication, conflicts, and collective decisions. This paper proposes an Explainable Decision Graph (EDG) framework for representing the reasoning process of autonomous multi-agent systems in a structured and interpretable form. The proposed framework models agents, observations, evi-dence, communications, intermediate decisions, conflicts, verifi-cation events, and final actions as interconnected graph com-ponents. A verification layer enables decision pathways to be examined against predefined safety and policy constraints. The resulting graph can provide different levels of explanations for end users, developers, and auditors. The paper defines an experimental methodology using multi-agent execution traces and proposes evaluation through ex-planation fidelity, completeness, decision traceability, human comprehensibility, decision accuracy, explanation consistency, and computational overhead. Empirical numerical results are intentionally reserved for the implementation and evaluation stage.

items.title: Financial self efficacy as a mediator of artificial intelligence use in detecting money laundering and financial fraud in Jordanian Islamic banks
items.abstract: This study examines the mediating role of financial self-efficacy in the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and the perceived effectiveness of detecting money laundering and financial fraud in Jordanian Islamic banks. The study addresses a behavioral and institutional gap in the literature by explaining how AI-supported monitoring capabilities may be translated into effective regulatory action through employees’ confidence in interpreting and using AI-generated outputs. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was adopted. Data were collected from 115 employees working in compliance, Shariah compliance, Shariah supervision, internal audit, auditing, and risk management functions in Jordanian Islamic banks. The questionnaire consisted of 35 items measuring AI adoption, financial self-efficacy, perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness, and demographic characteristics. The data were analyzed using reliability and validity tests, correlation analysis, standardized multiple regression, and regression-based mediation analysis. The results indicate that AI adoption has a statistically significant positive direct effect on perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness after accounting for financial self-efficacy (β = 0.296, p = 0.001). AI adoption also has a significant positive effect on financial self-efficacy ( β = 0.640, p < 0.001), while financial self-efficacy has a significant positive effect on perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness ( β = 0.491, p < 0.001). The mediation analysis shows a significant indirect effect of AI adoption on perceived detection effectiveness through financial self-efficacy (indirect effect = 0.314, Sobel z = 4.806, p < 0.001). The VAF value of 51.46% indicates complementary partial mediation. The findings suggest that AI adoption contributes to perceived AML/fraud detection effectiveness not only through technological capabilities but also through employees’ financial self-efficacy. The study recommends integrating AI-supported monitoring systems with structured training, human-in-the-loop governance, and Shariah-sensitive regulatory procedures in Islamic banks.

items.title: From “how” to learn to “what” to learn in multiagent systems and robotics
items.abstract: Abstract There remains much more to Artificial Intelligence than understanding how to learn with neural networks. Inspired in part by how babies, and humans in general, tend to choose for themselves what (and when ) to learn in addition to how to learn, this article discusses similar opportunities, in the areas of multiagent systems and robotics. Grounded in past research on the topic, it categorizes opportunities for choosing what to learn as coming from task decomposition or simplification for difficult problems and/or large environments; unsupervised pre‐training of representations and priors; multiagent learning; and learning from human interaction. The article is based closely on a keynote talk with the same title, delivered at the AAAI‐2026 conference in Singapore on January 22nd, 2026.

items.title: From AI labels to trust: cognitive pathways linking authenticity judgments, risk perception, and trust in AI-generated videos
items.abstract: Background The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) has raised concerns regarding the authenticity and trustworthiness of synthetic media. Although AI disclosure labels are increasingly used as transparency mechanisms, the cognitive processes through which these cues influence trust formation remain unclear. Objective This study aimed to develop and test a cognitive pathway model explaining how AI disclosure labels, authenticity judgments, perceived risk, cognitive processing styles, and literacy factors shape trust toward AI-generated videos. Methods A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 617 participants randomly assigned to four conditions involving AI-generated instructional videos with different AI label and video quality combinations. Participants evaluated authenticity, systematic and heuristic processing, trust, perceived risk, adoption intention, sharing intention, AI literacy, and media literacy. Regression, bootstrapped mediation, and moderation analyses were performed. Results AI disclosure labels significantly reduced perceived authenticity but did not directly affect trust, adoption, sharing intention, or perceived risk. Trust formation occurred through cognitive pathways: systematic processing increased trust, whereas heuristic processing reduced trust. Authenticity enhanced trust and lowered perceived risk, with perceived risk mediating the authenticity–trust relationship. Trust positively predicted adoption and sharing intentions, while AI and media literacy moderated selected relationships. Conclusion Trust in AI-generated videos was not directly determined by transparency labels alone. Instead, the observed associations among authenticity judgments, perceived risk, information processing, and trust were consistent with a multi-stage cognitive interpretation, although the cross-sectional post-exposure measurement of these constructs does not establish their temporal or causal sequence.

items.title: From AI models to AI agents: governance through recursive oversight and revocable access
items.abstract: Recent developments in AI are shifting the main source of risk from the flawed outputs of individual models to the unintended effects of agentic AI systems. Limited but growing evidence of misaligned behavior in swarms of AI agents suggests that such systems can pursue unassigned tasks and act beyond the reach of traditional corporate governance tools, which presuppose agents with interests, fiduciary duties and legal personality. This paper argues that the object of governance should be expanded from the model in isolation to the agentic AI system as a whole, and that oversight should be calibrated to the combined level of capability, autonomy, external access, permissions and scale. It proposes a framework of recursive governance, in which monitoring, evaluation, intervention and authorization form a continuous feedback loop rather than a fixed checklist. Four propositions follow: (P1) governance must become more stringent as capability and operational autonomy combine with external access and scale; (P2) autonomous deployment at a given capability level should not occur unless predefined criteria for evaluation, monitoring, containment and independent verification are met; (P3) some governance functions should be embedded in the technical architecture rather than being left solely to ex post human intervention; (P4) enforcement should rest on conditional and revocable access to the infrastructure that autonomous operation requires, with the kill switch as the last resort of a broader regime, and should be anchored as far as possible to institutions, rules and forms of self-regulation that already exist. To this end, the paper proposes a three-stage enforcement architecture: (i) a lean, independent multilateral agency, composed mainly of experts in advanced AI, certifies that the governance process for AI agents is actually followed; (ii) the certificate is fully incorporated into the ESG framework already operating in the European Union and linked to existing EU legislation on sustainability reporting, sustainable finance and ESG ratings; (iii) the IMF includes AI governance compliance in its periodic surveillance of member countries through the Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP). Apart from the new agency, which to our knowledge does not yet exist, enforcement would thus rely on institutions that are already in place. The proposed policies are framed as responses to three market failures: information asymmetry, negative externalities and a collective action problem among competing developers (a safety race to the bottom). The last of these is to be addressed through common safety standards, not through any relaxation of antitrust rules.

items.title: From AI-Assisted Performance to Independent Thinking: A Framework for Developing Higher-Order Thinking with Generative AI in Higher Education
items.abstract: In an AI-supported task, a student may explain a weak comparison once it has been identified, yet fail to notice a similar problem without a reminder. A decision about further help therefore needs evidence about what the student did without being prompted. We examine such decisions in English-medium university argumentation and evidence evaluation. The framework brings together English-language work on scaffolding, learner-generated reasoning, metacognitive calibration, and cognitive offloading. We distinguish help that supplies a reason from help that initiates a check. Readiness to work without the first does not establish readiness to work without the second. Coding examples and boundary cases make evidence about these functions interpretable, while six conditional propositions connect reconstruction and regulation to adaptation and transfer. A proposed experiment gives every group comparable diagnostic practice but varies whether teachers use its results to adjust assistance. This comparison isolates the value of using the evidence from learning through the diagnostic task itself. We relate the account to four GenAI approaches and illustrate it with a hypothetical sociology lesson. Help may be retained or restored when a new task requires it. The framework and coding rules need validation, particularly beyond the language and disciplinary settings considered here.

items.title: From disrupted routines to sustainable practice: integrating management sciences to navigate the innovation journey of precision imaging
items.abstract: Precision medicine is reshaping medical imaging through artificial intelligence, quantitative biomarkers or hybrid modalities such as PET-CT. Yet these tools reach patients unevenly, and that unevenness is usually blamed on technical problems: interoperability, validation, trust. Drawing on management science and the sociology of professions, we propose a different explanation. What decides whether an innovation reaches patients equitably is not the technology, but the way it travels. We distinguish three ways of travelling. Diffusion is spontaneous spread through professional networks (letting it happen). Dissemination is spread deliberately directed towards a defined population (helping it happen). Implementation is the work of turning an adopted innovation into everyday routine (making it happen). Imaging innovations have travelled mainly by diffusion, which follows existing specialist density, funding rules and like-with-like professional networks; diffusion therefore reproduces the inequalities of access it inherits instead of correcting them. Three consequences follow. First, adoption hides three separate decisions taken by different people: acquiring the equipment, deciding what the examination actually contains, and deciding whether it is requested at all. Routine statistics count the first and the third; the second is never measured. Second, professional boundaries are held in place at once by regulation, by specialty jurisdiction and by everyday working relationships, so reforms acting on only one of them fail. Third, the medical report is where those boundaries meet: when it does not carry an integrated answer, the innovation stalls. A fourth point runs through all three: an innovation's value is not fixed before it travels; its construction is predicated on the expectations that precede it, and the practices through which it is utilised. Using a three-study programme on PET-CT in France as illustration, we argue that equitable and sustainable precision imaging is achieved not by buying equipment but by governing how innovations spread—including by actively retiring the low-value practices they were meant to replace, what management science calls exnovation.

items.title: From joy to resistance: consumer reactions to disclosure of AI-created advertisements
items.abstract: Conventional wisdom suggests that viewers tend to evaluate AI-generated advertisements negatively. We argue that viewers can nevertheless enjoy creative advertisements produced by AI. However, the belief that creativity is an exclusively human attribute may prompt cognitive regulation when AI involvement is disclosed. Using a consumer neuroscience approach, we conducted a one-factor, three-level between-subjects experiment in which participants viewed advertisements with no disclosure, disclosure of human–AI collaboration, or disclosure of full AI creation. Creative advertisements elicited joy, captured by facial expression analysis, regardless of whether they were created by humans or AI. Greater joy was associated with less message counterarguing and more favourable advertisement attitudes, but only in the absence of AI disclosure. These findings suggest that AI disclosure does not diminish initial enjoyment. Instead, it may act as a persuasion knowledge cue that activates cognitive regulation, leading viewers to override their positive affective responses when subsequently evaluating the advertisement.

items.title: From Prompting to Direct Manipulation: Interaction Patterns and Designer Experience in Generative AI-Supported Visual Workflows
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now employed in many visual design programs to create images rapidly, but these images may not meet the designer's expectations at first glance. This paper studies mismatch via text prompting, parameters and presets, reference-based input, and in-canvas manipulation. The fourteen academic sources in the review include thirteen peer-reviewed publications from 2024-2026 and Shneiderman's original work on direct manipulation. The workflow stage, participant group, interaction pattern, and the five dimensions of efficiency, perceived control, cognitive load, creative agency, and output predictability were used for evidence coding. Based on this evidence, the demand for refinement reduces the apparent advantage of rapid exploration. Effort saved in generation may be recovered by reducing prompt modifications, filtering output, or re-retrieving a suitable image. More local interactions help express and observe the decisions, but they do not eliminate the uncertainty in the generated results. Evidence for the parameters and presets is relatively scarce, so all four patterns cannot be evaluated equally. This framing clarifies how interface design, rather than model capability alone, affects professional agency and supports more informed tool selection in creative practice.

items.title: Future Machines on the Moon: Robotic Autonomy, Human Supervision and the Emerging Security Dimension of Lunar Operations
items.abstract: Lunar exploration has shifted from single flights to a planned buildup of permanent infrastructure. NASA flew four astronauts around the Moon on Artemis II in April 2026, and within eight weeks announced the first three robotic Moon Base missions along with close to a billion dollars in contracts for surface rovers, cargo landers and hopping drones. A parallel programme led by China and Russia, the International Lunar Research Station, is working towards a basic configuration by 2035 with a nuclear power unit delivered between 2033 and 2035. This paper examines the machines that will carry out most of the work in both programmes. It sets out the supervised autonomy model that governs how humans and robots divide decisions under communication delay, identifies the specific artificial intelligence techniques that lunar robots depend on, and proposes an interaction protocol for surface operations. The paper then turns to security. Nearly every capability needed for lunar construction, survey and resource extraction has an obvious military application, and the argument advanced here is that any confrontation on the Moon would be short, machine-led and fought over access to a small number of usable sites rather than over territory in the terrestrial sense. Gaps in the Outer Space Treaty and in the Artemis Accords are assessed against that prospect.

items.title: Gamificación y motivación estudiantil: desafíos y oportunidades
items.abstract: Introduction: Gamification incorporates game design elements into educational activities and offers opportunities to strengthen student participation. However, its effects depend on planning, curricular objectives and implementation conditions. The aim was to analyse its relationship with student motivation and identify opportunities and challenges relevant to Ecuadorian upper secondary education. Methodology: A narrative review of twenty publications on motivational foundations, gamification and learning was developed, incorporating international contributions and a review situated in Ecuador. The synthesis addressed four dimensions: foundations, motivation, pedagogical opportunities and implementation challenges. Published findings were distinguished from teaching guidance derived from their interpretation. Results: The reviewed meta-analyses report favourable, although variable, effects on cognitive, motivational and behavioural outcomes. Evidence specifically concerning intrinsic motivation indicates a small effect, alongside improvements in autonomy and relatedness and a smaller effect on perceived competence. Feedback, progressive challenges and collaboration offer pedagogical possibilities, whereas controlling rewards, exclusionary competition, access barriers and assessment restricted to points require attention. Conclusions: Gamification can enrich teaching when game elements are linked to verifiable learning and inclusive participation opportunities. Its application to Ecuadorian upper secondary education requires contextual adaptation and assessment of understanding and sustained motivation. The narrative approach and diversity of sources limit generalisation and do not permit attribution of effects to specific institutions or causal conclusions about the Ecuadorian school context.

items.title: Generative AI and Social Inequality in Education: A Human-Centered Social Science Review of Global and Indonesian Evidence
items.abstract: This review examined how generative artificial intelligence (AI) can widen educational opportunity while also reproducing social inequality. An integrative review synthesized 24 sources: 17 Indonesian publications (2022–2026), identified through national journal portals and Google Scholar, and seven international policy documents and scholarly works (2016–2023) selected as conceptual anchors. Thematic analysis produced four themes: unequal access, unequal digital and AI literacy, unequal capacity to benefit from AI-supported learning, and governance risks involving privacy, bias, academic integrity, and human agency. The reported benefits of generative AI, such as tutoring, writing support, and translation, appear to depend on connectivity, devices, language resources, teacher competence, and students' ability to evaluate machine output. The Indonesian evidence is mostly cross-sectional, self-reported, or based on small single-institution samples, with little evidence on learning outcomes. One national household analysis of school participation (not AI use) found no significant difference between 3T (disadvantaged, frontier, and outermost) and matched non-3T households, suggesting that regional labels may be an imperfect proxy for household conditions. The review proposes a cumulative model of AI inequality that extends van Dijk's sequence of digital inequality with a governance stage and a feedback loop. The model is a conceptual proposition, not a tested result, and recommendations are ordered by the strength of supporting evidence.

items.title: Generative AI as a team moderator in CSCL : Facilitating students' multidimensional engagement through adaptive scaffolding for socially shared regulation of learning
items.abstract: Abstract Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is essential for successful collaboration, yet effectively scaffolding it remains challenging because regulatory needs are dynamic and context‐dependent. While generative AI (GenAI) offers potential for adaptive support, current applications in collaborative learning largely position it as a content‐oriented tutor for knowledge explanation or idea generation, leaving its role as a process‐oriented team moderator for scaffolding SSRL processes underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a 16‐week quasi‐experiment with 64 undergraduates in China, comparing adaptive SSRL scaffolding delivered by a GenAI agent in the adaptive‐SSRL condition with static scaffolding via structured digital worksheets in the static‐SSRL condition. Survey data and group discussion transcripts were analysed using statistical methods and epistemic network analysis. Results indicated several differences in students' multidimensional engagement between the two conditions: (1) Behaviourally, the adaptive‐SSRL group showed significantly higher participation equality, although participation intensity did not differ significantly between groups. (2) Cognitively, the adaptive‐SSRL group demonstrated deeper cognitive engagement, reflected in more advanced cognitive presence phases and more integrative, solution‐oriented discourse patterns. (3) Emotionally, the adaptive‐SSRL group reported significantly higher overall emotional engagement, particularly feeling more relaxed during collaboration and more connected with peers. These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by showing that GenAI can function as an SSRL‐informed team moderator rather than a content‐oriented tutor. They also offer design implications for GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding and human–AI role division in CSCL. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is critical for successful collaboration and is closely associated with the quality of student engagement. While static scaffolds (eg, worksheets) provide a basic regulatory structure, they fail to adapt to the dynamic and emergent needs of collaborating teams. Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used for personalised content support, yet its potential as a process‐oriented team moderator remains underexplored. What this paper adds This study introduced SSRLAgent, a GenAI agent grounded in SSRL theory and established principles of collective metacognitive support, to provide adaptive and interactive regulatory scaffolding. In a 16‐week quasi‐experiment, we compared GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding (SSRLAgent) with static scaffolding (structured digital worksheets) in CSCL. Adaptive‐SSRL scaffolding was associated with higher‐quality engagement: greater participation equality, deeper cognitive engagement and higher overall emotional engagement. Implications for practice and/or policy The study underscores the necessity of shifting SSRL scaffolding from static, ‘one‐size‐fits‐all’ support to adaptive GenAI interventions to improve collaborative engagement. The findings provide design guidance for developing SSRL agents that are embedded in the shared interaction space and responsive to groups' moment‐to‐moment regulatory needs. The study suggests a productive human–AI division of labour: GenAI agents can support process coordination and regulatory prompting, while teachers and peers remain essential for relationally complex forms of support that collaborative learning requires.

items.title: Generative AI Driven Cultural Content Production Mechanisms and Creative Labor Substitution Effects
items.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping content production in the cultural and creative industries by shifting cultural material organization, script writing, exhibition interpretation, and cultural tourism communication from linear manual workflows to human-AI collaborative workflows. Focusing on productivity improvement and the boundary of creative labor substitution, this research constructs a three-group comparison framework involving human-only creation, AI-assisted creation, and fully AI-generated creation. Based on public cultural heritage data, cultural policy texts, and cultural tourism communication samples from 2018 to 2024, LLMs, RAG, Sentence-BERT semantic retrieval, expert scoring, and mixed-effects ANOVA are combined to measure generation quality, policy suitability, and substitution intensity across different cultural tasks. The results show that the average completion time of the AI-assisted group decreases from 44.2 min to 25.7 min, while the overall quality score increases from 82.6 to 84.1, indicating that human-AI collaboration can improve production efficiency while maintaining content quality. Although the fully AI-generated group achieves the lowest time cost, its policy suitability and cultural accuracy decline noticeably. Task complexity further affects substitution intensity. Cultural tourism copy and short-video scripts are more substitutable, while exhibition interpretation and policy explanation still rely on human judgment. These findings provide quantitative evidence for AI adoption, creative labor restructuring, and cultural policy governance.

items.title: Generative AI in clinical practice: how should rheumatologists evaluate and monitor emerging tools?
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in rheumatology practice, to assist with tasks such as documentation, record summarization, and clinical decision support. Rheumatologists need a practical approach to determining what evidence and oversight each application requires. This narrative review proposes a framework based on two dimensions: contextual complexity and influence on patient care. Greater contextual complexity can make errors harder to detect, whereas greater influence on care increases the potential consequences of an undetected error. We examine evidence for workflow benefits and clinical effectiveness within this framework and consider safety, equity, privacy, governance, and implementation. Existing evidence on the benefits, accuracy and reliability of AI applications remains mixed. For example, studies of ambient AI scribes suggest reduced documentation burden, but evidence of improved patient outcomes from applications supporting clinical decisions is more limited. For applications with limited clinical influence, evaluation has initially focused on workflow, usability, and documentation quality. Tools that synthesize longitudinal information require additional assessment of completeness and source traceability. Those influencing diagnosis or treatment require prospective evaluation of clinical benefit and safety. Relevant vendor evidence should be assessed alongside proportionate local testing and ongoing monitoring. Safeguards should address risks such as hallucinations, automation bias, and propagating documentation errors, with attention to performance across patient groups. Changes in functionality or clinical use should prompt reassessment. The framework provides a structured basis for adoption decisions and identifies priorities for research on patient outcomes and feasible oversight in routine rheumatology care.

items.title: Generative AI Tools for Performance Assessment of University Students: Effects, Challenges, and Countermeasures
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of educational evaluation reform, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) has been increasingly applied to performance assessment, yet its actual effects and challenges remain underexplored. This study surveyed 50 undergraduate students to examine their perceptions of GAI-based performance assessment across five dimensions: evaluation efficiency and feedback timeliness, accuracy and fairness, appropriateness of scoring criteria and weight distribution, stability and trust, and deep learning and innovation. Results show that over 70% of respondents recognized GAI's advantages in scoring speed and feedback timeliness, and most regarded its scoring criteria as clear and consistent. However, nearly 75% believed GAI failed to identify innovative highlights, over 70% perceived a tendency to emphasize form over content, and 44% reported that such preferences constrained their creative expression. Respondents also raised concerns about incorrect information, technical instability, and the lack of emotional interaction compared with human evaluation. These findings suggest that GAI should act as an auxiliary tool rather than a full replacement for teacher evaluation. To address current limitations, it is necessary to improve GAI's deep evaluation and fact-checking capabilities, establish human-machine collaborative review mechanisms, and cultivate students' critical thinking. This study provides implications for integrating GAI into university performance assessment.

items.title: Generative AI-related employment threat, AI optimism, and employment anxiety among domestic and international students at a Chinese university
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the labor market, yet it remains unclear whether students’ appraisal of AI-driven employment threat translates into employment anxiety in similar ways across cultural groups. This study administered an online questionnaire to 1,595 domestic students (1,095) and international students (500) enrolled at Central South University. Perceived AI replacement threat, AI optimism, and employment anxiety were assessed with 13 five-point Likert items. Information channels, coping behaviors, desired institutional support, and perceived coping relief were assessed as supplementary measures. Confirmatory factor analyses supported an acceptable three-factor structure in both groups. The distinction between threat and anxiety remained qualified due to their substantial association. Metric invariance was established, and partial scalar invariance was obtained after the intercept of Q21 was freed. Perceived AI replacement threat and employment anxiety remained empirically distinguishable, although their latent correlation was stronger among international students than among domestic students. In the structural model, threat was strongly associated with anxiety ( β = 0.764) and weakly associated with optimism ( β = 0.133). After threat was included, optimism showed a small negative conditional association with anxiety ( β = −0.152). The indirect association through optimism was negative but limited in magnitude, and equivalent cross-sectional specifications fit the data equally well. This pattern is best interpreted as an exploratory statistical finding compatible with suppression, rather than confirmed evidence of a directional psychological mechanism. Supplementary coping analyses were descriptive and exploratory. These findings provide qualified empirical support for a three-factor framework of students’ responses to AI-related employment uncertainty, and highlight differences in threat-anxiety coupling across student populations. The results carry implications for targeted student support services addressing AI-related career concerns.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence use and interpersonal educational interaction among nursing students: self-regulated learning as a statistical mediator
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is reshaping health sciences education. For nursing students, educational interaction (EI), self-regulated learning (SRL), and GAI interaction are all particularly important. However, these relationships and their processes remain underexplored. Methods A total of 1020 nursing students were recruited from one medical university in Hunan Province in China. The Demographics Questionnaire, the Chinese version of Student-GAI interaction scale, the Educational Interaction Scale, and the Self-regulated Learning Questionnaire were administered. SPSS 22.0 and AMOS 24.0 software were used to analyze the data. Results The mean scores of student-GAI interaction (SGI) and EI were 14.80 ± 2.27 and 70.90 ± 8.15, respectively. Significant positive relationships were found among all three variables (all P < 0.01). Both SGI (β = 0.256) and SRL (β = 0.520) positively were associated with EI (both P < 0.001). Furthermore, SGI showed a significant direct association with EI, with a direct effect value of 0.92 ( P < 0.001). SRL statistically mediated the association between SGI and EI, with a significant indirect effect value of 0.44. The mediating effect represented 32.35% of the total effect ( P < 0.001). Dimension-specific analyses revealed that the mediating effect was strongest for student-teacher interaction (45.41%) and student-content interaction (41.54%). Conclusions SGI is positively associated with EI among nursing students, both directly and indirectly through SRL. Educational strategies that encourage effective GAI use and strengthen SRL may be associated with enhanced EI in nursing education.

items.title: Groundhog Loops: A Time-Loop Testbed for Measuring Learning Speed and Tactic Formation in AI Agents
items.abstract: The project defines a test environment inspired by the time-loop mechanism featured in the film Groundhog Day. An agent attempts to complete a task; if it makes an error classified as fatal (or exhausts its step budget), the environment is restored to a previously saved checkpoint, while the agent retains a complete, structured memory of all previous loops: the loop counter, cumulative time, summaries of failed attempts, and its own hypotheses. Unlike a conventional episode reset in reinforcement learning (RL), failure information is not lost—it becomes a persistent part of the agent's observations. Additionally, after a reset, the environment may slightly mutate the task conditions, but only when necessary to force the agent to change its strategy (the minimal-intervention principle). These mutations are observable to the agent but are never explicitly signaled. Project objectives: - C1. Build a measurable benchmark for agents' ability to perform within-episode meta-learning (in-context adaptation across resets): the agent should learn from failures without updating its weights. - C2. Investigate whether explicit loop memory reduces time to success compared with an agent without memory (control-group experiments). - C3. Investigate whether minimal changes to task conditions disrupt strategy lock-in, i.e., a situation in which an agent repeatedly attempts variations of the same flawed strategy despite having complete memory of its failures. - C4. Provide a reproducible, deterministic (seeded) harness for experiments with RL agents and LLM-based agents, using a single, unified evaluation protocol. - C5. Identify and measure undesirable emergent behaviors: reward hacking through deliberately triggering resets, learned helplessness, and overfitting to the mutation pattern. Out of scope: gradient-based weight training across loops (the project evaluates in-context adaptation through memory, not through-gradient meta-learning); physical real-time simulation. items.title: Hacia una ética proléptica: experiencia, anticipación e inteligencia artificial
items.abstract: This article presents the results of a theoretical-conceptual study based on a critical analysis of the relevant philosophical literature. The central concepts were traced across the philosophical literature and, on the basis of that analysis, ethical prolepsis is proposed as an attitude of the operative subject toward the foreseeable consequences of their actions, an attitude grounded in accumulated experience and constitutively practical in its orientation, that is, always referred to effective courses of action rather than to formal principles detached from praxis. It is found that, although the anticipatory disposition can be identified at various points in the Western philosophical tradition, it has in no case received a formulation that situates it as an ethical attitude of primary standing, and it is precisely that omission which this work aims to help redress. As part of the proposal, the manifestations of the proleptic attitude are established at the individual and social levels, and its specific relevance to the phenomenon of artificial intelligence (AI) is argued, with attention to the problem of anthropomorphization, whose epistemic and moral consequences are briefly examined in relation to epistemic agency, moral agency, responsibility gaps, and biocomputation.

items.title: How L2 selves shape attitudes toward AI-assisted language learning: the mediating roles of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation in cross-cultural Asian contexts
items.abstract: Introduction This study investigates the relationship between the L2 motivational self-system and attitudes toward AI-enhanced second language (L2) learning, and tests whether intrinsic and extrinsic motivation mediate these relationships among students learning Chinese or English as a foreign language in Thailand, Macau, and Mainland China. Methods Questionnaire data were collected from 361 participants. Correlational analysis, hierarchical regression, and a bootstrapping approach were used to test mediational relations. Results Both the ought-to L2 self and the ideal L2 self were significantly associated with attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning, with the ideal L2 self showing the stronger association. In the overall sample, and in the Thai and Mainland Chinese samples analyzed separately, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation statistically fully mediated the association between the ought-to L2 self and attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning. In the Macau sample, extrinsic motivation was more involved than intrinsic motivation in transmitting this effect. For the ideal L2 self, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation only partially mediated the relationship with attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning. Discussion Positive attitudes toward AI-enhanced L2 learning are not formed merely through future self-representations; they are also linked to learners’ intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. By examining the interaction between the L2 motivational self-system and intrinsic and extrinsic motivation across different regions, this study extends L2 motivation research to the area of AI-enhanced language learning.

items.title: Human-Centered AI Metacognition: Development and Validation of a Scale for Preserving Cognitive Autonomy in Human–AI Collaboration
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming human cognitive activities and creating a growing need to preserve cognitive autonomy in human–AI interactions. Although recent research has examined metacognition in AI-mediated environments, existing work has primarily focused on improving AI use and human–AI collaboration, with less attention to how individuals regulate the role and extent of AI involvement in their own cognitive activities. To address this gap, the present study introduced Human-Centered AI Metacognition (HC-AIM), defined as the capacity to recognize AI capabilities and limitations, monitor AI-generated information, and regulate the extent to which AI participates in one’s own cognitive activities while maintaining cognitive autonomy. Across three studies, we developed the Chinese version of the Human-Centered AI Metacognition Scale (HC-AIMS) and conducted an initial psychometric evaluation. Study 1 examined the scale structure using exploratory factor analysis and supported a predominantly unidimensional structure with good internal consistency. Study 2 examined this structure using confirmatory factor analysis and provided evidence of its convergent validity through its association with general metacognition. Study 3 further replicated the scale structure and internal consistency and examined its relationships with AI literacy, collaborative AI metacognition, and autonomous cognitive offloading. HC-AIM was positively associated with all three constructs. Comparisons of theoretically specified factor models provided preliminary evidence of empirical distinguishability between HC-AIM and both AI literacy and collaborative AI metacognition, despite substantial correlations with these constructs. HC-AIM was also positively associated with autonomous cognitive offloading, providing complementary self-reported criterion-related evidence for its validity. Taken together, the findings suggest that HC-AIM represents a contextualized, human-centered form of metacognitive regulation that is closely related to broader metacognitive and AI-related competencies while specifically emphasizing the regulation of AI participation in human cognition. The Chinese version of the HC-AIMS provides a theoretically grounded starting point for investigating human cognition and cognitive autonomy in AI-mediated environments.

items.title: Humans Correct Their Judgments Through Debate, but Weaker AI Models Do Not
items.abstract: How can we effectively oversee AI systems that surpass human intelligence? AI Safety via Debate proposes that two AI systems argue opposing positions and a judge, either a human or a weaker model, decides which is correct. By facilitating supervisors in providing high-quality training signals, debate aims to encourage truthful and safe behavior from AI systems whose capabilities exceed our own. However, human judgment is not neutral: people often rely on biases which advanced AI systems may learn to exploit. Drawing on insights from collective intelligence and social cognition, this paper investigates whether debate can guide human and LLM supervisors toward the truth despite their prior beliefs. We evaluate several protocol configurations. We also explore setups inspired by the wisdom of the crowd such as the number and diversity of judges, as well as interaction mechanisms including deliberation and voting. Overall, we find that debate increases accuracy relative to prior beliefs for human judges, whereas the consultancy baseline, in which a single expert argues for one answer, does not. For weaker language models, however, the results are mixed: debate provides no comparable gains in most settings and can even reduce accuracy. Among multi-judge protocols, weighted voting produces the highest accuracy for human supervisors, whereas for LLMs none of them significantly improves group accuracy, even as the number of judges increases. Notably, the behavior of minority judges in non-diverse deliberation protocols suggests that, under symmetric settings, incorrect positions could be more persuasive than correct ones. These findings support debate as a viable path toward scalable human oversight, but cast doubt on its benefits for weaker AI supervisors, raising concerns about fully automated training and control pipelines in high-stakes settings.

items.title: IMPACT OF EMOTIONAL AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AMONG ADOLESCENCE AND ADULTS
items.abstract: The present study aimed to examine differences in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Emotional Intelligence (EI) between adolescents and adults, investigate gender differences, and explore the relationship between AI and EI. The study included 120 participants, comprising 60 adolescents and 60 adults. Data were analysed using the t-test and Pearson’s product-moment correlation coefficient. The findings revealed no statistically significant differences between adolescents and adults in Artificial Intelligence (t = 0.38) or Emotional Intelligence (t = 0.93) at the 0.05 significance level. Similarly, no significant gender differences were observed in Emotional Intelligence (t = 0.39) or Artificial Intelligence (t = 1.70). Furthermore, the correlation analysis indicated a negligible negative relationship between Artificial Intelligence and Emotional Intelligence (r = −0.056, p = 0.543), which was statistically insignificant. These findings suggest that the studied groups exhibited broadly similar scores across the examined variables, with no significant association between AI and EI. The study highlights the importance of understanding the psychological implications of increasing AI use among different age groups and genders. Further research with larger and more diverse samples is recommended to explore the complex relationship between technological engagement and emotional functioning.

items.title: IMPACT OF PEDAGOGICAL TECHNOLOGY INTEGRATION ON TERTIARY LEARNERS’ BEHAVIOURAL ENGAGEMENT DURING TASK EXECUTION
items.abstract: This study examines the technology-integrated instructions’ impact on tertiary students’ behavioural engagement during the task execution. Two main theoretical models were used to explore the independent variable - teachers’ technology integration and the dependent variable ‘behavioural engagement’ during the learning activity. The first construct, pedagogical integration, is premised upon the SAMR model, while the second construct is based on the Fredricks, Blumenfeld, and Paris (2004) three - dimensional engagement model - behavioural, emotional and cognitive engagement. The study sampled 535 Arabic-speaking English language learners from arts and science backgrounds enrolled in the Foundation Year programme at a public university in Saudi Arabia. A self-developed questionnaire consisting of 32 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale measured both constructs. The findings show that the statistical assumptions necessary for the analysis were met, allowing for reliable modeling. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) revealed that technology engagement (TE) is best measured as a unidimensional construct, while the pedagogical use of technology (PUT) is multidimensional. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) confirmed a one-factor model for TE and a four-factor model for PUT, with the second-order PUT model providing the best fit. Additionally, the findings highlighted that strategic technology integration by instructors enhances learner engagement even in challenging conditions such as fatigue. items.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence And Personality Traits Into The Theory Of Planned Behavior: Driving Shariah Compliant Investment Decisions
items.abstract: This study aims to examine a structural framework integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Personality Traits into the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) model, with intention acting as a mediating variable on Shariah investment decisions among Generation Z in Indonesia. Data analysis was conducted using a quantitative approach with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that TPB has a positive and significant effect on investment intention. Intention also strongly mediates the relationship between TPB and investment decisions and has a significant direct impact on actual investment decisions. Conversely, AI and Personality Traits do not significantly influence investment intention, and intention fails to mediate the effect of these variables on investment decisions. The study concludes that for Generation Z investors, external stimuli, social trends, and platform accessibility reflected in the TPB model dominate the decision-making process far more than intrinsic personality factors or pure AI algorithmic features that lack human validation for Shariah compliance. Therefore, the Islamic capital market industry is advised to prioritize the development of social ecosystems and user-friendly application designs.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial en psiquiatría: usos y promesas
items.abstract: This article examines the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into psychiatry, highlighting both its transformative potential and its ethical, clinical, and philosophical challenges. AI applications (ranging from diagnostic algorithms and predictive models to therapeutic chatbots and neuroimplants) are reshaping mental healthcare by improving early detection, personalizing treatments, and expanding access to services, particularly in resource-limited settings. Advanced techniques such as machine learning and natural language processing enable the analysis of multimodal data, enhancing clinical decision-making and enabling preventive interventions. However, the adoption of AI raises significant concerns. These include risks to privacy, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, and challenges in ensuring informed consent, particularly in vulnerable psychiatric populations. Neurotechnologies such as deep brain stimulation (DBS), especially when assisted by AI, introduce further ethical dilemmas related to autonomy, identity, and long-term safety. The article argues that these challenges cannot be addressed without a deeper conceptual understanding of mental disorders. It advocates for a pluralistic and enactivist framework, which views mental health conditions as dynamic interactions between brain, body, and environment. Ultimately, the responsible integration of AI in psychiatry requires robust ethical governance, interdisciplinary collaboration, and a human-centered approach.

items.title: INTUITION AND MECHANISMS OF ITS KNOWLEDGE IN THE CONTEXT OF MODERN CYBERNETICS AND THE THEORY OF COMPLEX SYSTEMS
items.abstract: This article presents the fundamental foundations and specific characteristics of intuition, as well as the mechanisms for its comprehension, particularly within the framework of cybernetics and complex systems theory. Today, intuition is understood in science as a multi-level and complex phenomenon, the process of cognition of which includes both rational and irrational components. The authors convincingly argue that intuition has its own structure and a certain logic; it can be considered within the framework of nonlinear dynamics as a self-organizing system with feedback and multiple mechanisms. The analysis shows that intuitive knowledge arises where research encounters high rates of change not only in the environment but also in its component parts, incomplete empirical data, and a lack of resources. As is well known, the concept of “observer” is introduced within the paradigm of post-non-classical science, particularly within the context of the evolutionary-constructive model of scientific knowledge development. Now the observer is directly viewed as part of the system, and their intuitive decisions are perceived as the result of the interaction of internal cognitive structures with external information flows. As a result, it becomes possible to interpret intuition as a significant factor in cognition, capable of minimizing the tacitness and uncertainty of knowledge. Thus, intuition becomes a natural and objective regulator of the formation of new knowledge through the synthesis of heterogeneous information. Intuition and its mechanisms are well suited to the theory of complex systems. In particular, the phenomenon of self-organization, especially emergence in intuition, is a nonlinear interaction between system elements, resulting in transitions between different cognitive states and the formation of qualitatively new types of knowledge. Research demonstrates how and by what means parallels arise between human intuition and constructed models, how weak and implicit signals are recognized, and how intuitive probabilistic predictions are formed. Conclusion: Intuition is a unique phenomenon, a special adaptive mechanism for knowledge processing, essential for the successful functioning of humans and intelligent systems in the context of the nonequilibrium of the modern world and the increasing complexity of cognitive processes, encompassing both physical reality and the metaphysics of existence. This approach offers new prospects for the development of hybrid human-machine systems, where intuitive and rational mechanisms interact as complementary modes of cognition.

items.abstract: The Physical Limit of Capital: Energy, Infrastructure and Geopolitics in the New Resource Economy ISHEA Premiere Report · Vol. 1, No. 1 · September 2026 This report examines the relationship between financial capital, physical resource availability, infrastructure resilience, and geopolitical risk in the global economy. It explores how the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure, the reconfiguration of energy and mineral supply chains, and the strategic transformation of maritime and logistics corridors are reshaping the conditions under which financial value can be converted into realizable economic activity. Using an interdisciplinary analytical framework informed by biophysical accounting, bioenergetics, cognitive economics, complex systems, and resilience analysis, the report examines three interconnected dimensions: the physical infrastructure supporting AI-related investment; the strategic role of energy resources and logistics corridors in international capital allocation; and the implications of geopolitical disruption for asset valuation and business planning. The report introduces an ISHEA analytical heuristic, Realizable Value, which considers financial value alongside physical availability, logistical resilience, and flow security. This formulation is presented as a diagnostic framework rather than a calibrated or empirically validated valuation model. The report concludes with practical recommendations for business planning in 2026–2027, including physical-dependency audits, geographic and supplier redundancy, energy-risk assessment, and systemic stress testing. Purpose: To contribute to interdisciplinary discussion on the relationship between financial valuation and the physical, infrastructural, and geopolitical conditions that sustain economic activity. items.abstract: WHEN A DEGREE IS NO LONGER A PROMISE A Conditional Foresight Essay on Education, Employment, and Human Life-Cycle Transition Infrastructure Author: Bùi Quang TrịnhIndependent Researcher, VietnamFounder, Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Abstract This conditional foresight essay explores possible transformations in education, employment, professional identity, and social institutions as artificial intelligence, automation, and rapidly changing economic structures reshape the relationship between human knowledge and work. Developed within the Boundary Information Theory (BIT) research programme, the essay asks whether future civilization will be able to maintain meaningful transitions between learning, professional contribution, personal development, and a dignified human life. The essay presents nine conditional future perspectives. First, academic degrees may increasingly function as evidence of educational achievement rather than implicit guarantees of specific professional positions. Second, automation and artificial intelligence may reduce certain entry-level tasks, potentially weakening traditional pathways through which younger generations acquire professional experience. Third, institutions may develop transferable capability profiles that recognize practical skills, interdisciplinary competence, and demonstrated problem-solving ability beyond conventional occupational titles. Fourth, universities may expand their responsibilities by supporting graduates through longer professional transitions rather than ending institutional support at graduation. Fifth, countries may begin treating unused human expertise as a potential public resource, creating mechanisms to connect available capabilities with unmet social needs. Sixth, careers may increasingly involve multiple transitions among employment, education, independent work, care responsibilities, and periods of recovery. Seventh, artificial intelligence may improve labor-market matching while simultaneously creating new risks of algorithmic exclusion, opacity, and unfair screening. Eighth, future institutions may recognize periods of unemployment, retraining, caregiving, and independent research as legitimate phases of human development rather than treating them as personal deficiencies. Ninth, the evaluation of education and employment policies may shift toward their long-term effects on the complete human life cycle, including health, family formation, professional resilience, social participation, and security in later life. Central Proposition The future value of education may depend not only on academic credentials, but also on whether civilization develops effective bridges between human learning, meaningful contribution, and dignified life transitions. The essay suggests that education, employers, governments, and technological systems may need to share responsibility for maintaining these pathways. Scope and Limitations This publication is a conditional foresight essay, not a probabilistic forecast or an empirically established prediction. It does not claim that academic degrees will necessarily lose their value, that artificial intelligence will inevitably eliminate entry-level employment, or that one institutional model will suit every society. The possibilities discussed may emerge differently across countries, economic sectors, and social groups. The purpose is to contribute to public reflection and interdisciplinary research on education, artificial intelligence, employment transitions, institutional design, and human-centered civilization. items.title: Knowing When to Hand Over: A Survey of Uncertainty, Deferral, and Escalation in Human–AI Fraud Investigation
items.abstract: Language-model agents are being proposed to investigate fraud and money-laundering alerts under selective autonomy: the agent closes some cases itself and escalates the rest to a human analyst. Which cases it escalates determines the division of labor, the analysts' workload, and the errors that reach customers and regulators, yet the knowledge needed to design that rule is divided among learning to defer and selective prediction, uncertainty estimation for language models, and research on human reliance on AI advice. This survey connects the three through the escalation loop of a fraud-investigation team and restates known results from these literatures in one notation. We state the cost-optimal escalation rule, which requires different confidence thresholds for closing a case as benign and for concluding fraud, and its form under a fixed analyst capacity; show that calibration suffices for selective risk to be monotone and interpretable; state the conformal bound on the rate of cases that are both closed automatically and wrong; show when combining uncertainty signals helps and when correlated signals double-count; show that the error among automatically closed cases is not identified without audits and is estimable with them; and quantify how analyst reliance on the agent's verdict erodes the value of escalation. Against this basis we compare deferral rules and uncertainty signals, and conclude that threshold-based deferral rules assume a calibrated confidence that agents do not yet provide, that agent-level uncertainty estimation is only beginning, and that, to our knowledge, no peer-reviewed study has yet evaluated an escalation rule for a fraud-investigation agent together with the analysts who receive its cases.

items.title: La inteligencia artificial y sus implicaciones antihumanistas. Consecuencias de la delegación de la responsabilidad del pensar en las máquinas
items.abstract: Various voices warn of the growing anti-humanism that prevails today. This risk of the devaluation of humanity finds a salient example—in the context of posthumanism in its cybernetic form—in the unstoppable development of AI with the emergence of products such as ChatGPT, capable of generating literary, musical, or pictorial compositions. This is a technology that enables humans to delegate to non-thinking machines the responsibility for the task of thinking in its different domains—cognitive, evaluative, or artistic creation— thus running the risk of falling back, in Kantian terms, into a condition of immaturity. The task of thought—and, therefore, of philosophy—should consist in remaining vigilant in order to resist such temptations and, if possible, in exercising with greater firmness that faculty of thinking characteristic of humans, by analyzing the age in which they find themselves and the dangers that lie in wait for them.

items.title: Leveraging AI for Higher Education Human Resources:A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Human Resource Development (HRD) policies for academic staff in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) is often constrained by the misalignment between computational capabilities and institutional governance. While HEIs generate substantial datasets through the Tri Dharma (the three pillars of higher education: teaching, research, and community service), this data remains underutilized for proactive policy-making. To map the state-of-the-art and identify existing research gaps, this study conducts a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) and bibliometric analysis of 400 unique peer-reviewed documents, obtained from an initial 485 records retrieved from Scopus (n = 260) and Web of Science (n = 225) after removing 85 duplicates, covering the seven-year period from 2018 to 2024. Visual analysis using VOSviewer reveals a distinct semantic-policy discrepancy, showing that semantic technologies and predictive AI models are researched as isolated technical domains, seldom integrated into comprehensive institutional governance. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a framework for Higher Education Human Resources for Lecturer Career Development. The proposed framework integrates machine learning classifiers (Naïve Bayes, K-Means, and Apriori association) with a semantic Knowledge Graph layer to transform descriptive academic metrics into explainable, policy-conforming recommendations. Preliminary expert consultation with LLDIKTI Region II highlights the conceptual viability of the Framework for Higher Education Human Resources for Lecturer Career Development in mitigating administrative bottlenecks, supporting objective career path design, and minimizing human subjectivity in lecturer performance evaluations.

items.title: Looks Fine to Me: Understanding Oversight in Agentic Interactions
items.abstract: Agentic AI systems are deployed to execute complex tasks across domains such as writing, coding, and data analysis. As execution is offloaded to AI agents, the human role shifts toward oversight. Effective oversight requires recognizing when closer scrutiny is needed, even though flawed outputs may appear convincing. Our formative study (N=12) revealed that users accepted plausible outputs without thorough evaluation, and only recognized these lapses in retrospect. To examine this systematically, we conducted a controlled within-subject study (N=36) in which participants completed programming tasks with an agent that produced correct outputs, silent defects, or visible failures. Combining task outcomes, interaction logs, gaze, physiological signals, and self-reports, we examined perceived, behavioral, and effective oversight. Participants were often highly confident while missing silent defects: they performed generic checks, failed to generate diagnostic evidence, or even misinterpreted defect evidence. We discuss how studying oversight across multiple dimensions can support future work on timely, task-calibrated re-engagement.

items.abstract: Dialogic Artificial Intelligence (DAI) or communicative AI within Large Language Models (LLMs) is rapidly expanding across higher education and academic workflows in both teaching and research. The adoption of DAI is being driven by the pressure to enhance productivity and automate academic practices. This paper discusses the primary risks that the intensive use of DAI poses to human cognitive capacities, information biases, and the erosion of literacy, critical thinking, argumentation, and academic discourse skills. Furthermore, it analyzes emerging forms of plagiarism and misconduct facilitated by DAI while reflecting on the concept of individual authorship, which has become obsolete, giving way to human-AI co-authorship. As an immersive technology that impacts human agency and autonomy, DAI could irreversibly transform cognition, literacy, the sense of authorship, and collaborative frameworks in research, teaching, and scholarly production. Finally, it concludes with a set of criteria and recommendations to guide university regulatory policies on DAI, moving beyond prohibitions, punitive measures, or ineffective appeals to individual ethics in the use of LLMs.

items.title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.abstract: Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.

items.title: MMEnterprise-Bench: Evaluating Enterprise Agents over Evolving Multimodal Records
items.abstract: Enterprise agents answer questions over workplace records that evolve through team collaboration. As information is shared, corrected, and revised across documents, chats, and figures, multiple versions of the same information accumulate in the workspace. Reliable question answering therefore requires agents to reason over sufficient evidence, resolve cross-source and temporal conflicts, and recognize when the available evidence is insufficient to establish an answer. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce MMEnterprise-Bench, a benchmark comprising 1,613 questions grounded in evolving multimodal records from simulated collaboration projects, covering three categories: Evidence Reasoning, Conflict Resolution, and Unanswerability. We evaluate 10 proprietary and open-source multimodal LLMs and find that even the strongest models struggle when evidence contains cross-source or temporal conflicts or spans multiple images. Moreover, increasing the retrieval budget or employing a larger retriever improves evidence recall but does not consistently translate into higher answer accuracy. These findings highlight the persistent challenges of reasoning over evolving workplace records and establish MMEnterprise-Bench as a testbed for developing more reliable enterprise agents. Code and data are available at https://mlvlab.github.io/MMEnterprise-Bench/.
